notice: RN bank batch 27: Maternity II: labor, birth and fetal monitoring. Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: A client at 39 weeks calls the birthing unit at 0200 with contractions every 5 to 8 minutes for 3 hours, felt in the lower back and abdomen. The client is unsure whether to come in. Which finding at triage would best confirm true labor?

options.text: Cervix changed from 2 cm to 4 cm over 2 hours
Contractions that grow stronger when the client walks the hall
Bloody show seen on the perineal pad
Contractions felt as tightening across the abdomen

rationale.correct: True labor: regular contractions that grow stronger, longer and closer and progressively dilate and efface the cervix.

perOption.a: Only true labor produces progressive cervical change.
perOption.b: Contractions that intensify with walking suggest true labor, but cervical change is what confirms it.
perOption.c: Bloody show can occur days before labor begins.
perOption.d: False labor is commonly felt in the abdomen.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish true labor from false labor.

questions.stem: A client in labor has been pushing for 40 minutes, and the student nurse asks which stage of labor this is. The nurse explains that the second stage of labor lasts from which point to which point?

options.text: From full cervical dilation (10 cm) to the birth of the baby
From the onset of regular contractions to full dilation of the cervix
From the birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta
From delivery of the placenta to 4 hours after birth

rationale.correct: Stages: 1 (dilation), 2 (birth of the baby), 3 (placenta), 4 (recovery, 1 to 4 hours).

perOption.a: The second stage is the pushing and birth stage.
perOption.b: This is the first stage.
perOption.c: This is the third stage.
perOption.d: This is the fourth stage.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 38 weeks is admitted in early labor. Leopold maneuvers find a hard, round part at the pelvic inlet and a smooth, firm surface along the client's left side, and the vaginal exam confirms a left occiput anterior (LOA) position. Where should the nurse place the external fetal heart monitor?

options.text: Left lower quadrant, below the umbilicus
Right upper quadrant, above the umbilicus
Left upper quadrant, above the umbilicus
Right lower quadrant, over the fetal small parts

rationale.correct: Fetal heart tones are heard best over the fetal back: below the umbilicus in a vertex position and above it in a breech position.

perOption.a: In a head-down fetus with its back to the left, heart tones are loudest below the umbilicus on the left.
perOption.b: This suits a breech fetus with its back on the right.
perOption.c: This suits a breech fetus with its back on the left.
perOption.d: Heart tones are faint over the fetal limbs.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Locate fetal heart tones by fetal position.

questions.stem: A client at 7 cm dilation has a fetal heart rate baseline of 135/min with moderate variability. With each contraction, the rate gradually drops to 120/min, reaching its lowest point at the peak of the contraction and returning to baseline as it ends. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep monitoring, because these are early decelerations
Turn the client to the side and give an IV fluid bolus
Stop the oxytocin and notify the provider right away
Prepare the client for an emergency cesarean birth

rationale.correct: Early decelerations mirror the contraction and come from head compression; no action is needed.

perOption.a: Early decelerations come from head compression and need no intervention.
perOption.b: This is the response to late decelerations, which begin after the contraction peaks.
perOption.c: Early decelerations do not call for stopping oxytocin.
perOption.d: This pattern is benign.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 6 cm receiving oxytocin at 12 milliunits/min has contractions every 2 to 3 minutes. The fetal heart rate baseline is 150/min with minimal variability, and gradual decelerations begin after the peak of each of the last four contractions. The client is lying on the back. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the oxytocin infusion
Turn the client to the left side and recheck the tracing in 15 minutes
Apply oxygen at 10 L/min by nonrebreather mask
Ask the client to start pushing to speed the birth

rationale.correct: Late decelerations (uteroplacental insufficiency): stop oxytocin, reposition to the side, give an IV bolus, consider oxygen per protocol and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Stopping oxytocin reduces contractions and improves placental blood flow; repositioning, a fluid bolus and notifying the provider follow.
perOption.b: Repositioning helps, but oxytocin is still driving the contractions that cause the decelerations.
perOption.c: Oxygen may be used per protocol but does not remove the cause.
perOption.d: The client is not fully dilated.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 5 cm with ruptured membranes has a fetal heart rate tracing with abrupt, V-shaped drops to 90/min lasting 20 to 30 seconds, occurring with some contractions and not others. The baseline is 140/min with moderate variability. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Change the client's position
Increase the oxytocin to shorten the labor
Prepare for an emergency cesarean birth
Place the client flat on the back with the legs raised

rationale.correct: Variable decelerations: reposition, check for cord prolapse, stop oxytocin if recurrent and consider amnioinfusion.

perOption.a: Variable decelerations come from cord compression; a position change may relieve it.
perOption.b: Stronger contractions increase cord compression.
perOption.c: Intermittent variables with moderate variability do not call for this.
perOption.d: The supine position adds vena cava compression.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing four segments of a fetal heart rate tracing during the first stage of labor. For each pattern, indicate its most likely cause.

rows.text: A gradual drop that mirrors the contraction from start to finish
An abrupt V-shaped drop with no consistent timing
A gradual drop that begins after the contraction peaks
A rise of 15 beats/min for 20 seconds with fetal movement

rationale.correct: VEAL CHOP: Variable–Cord, Early–Head, Accelerations–OK, Late–Placenta.

perOption.r1:c1: Early decelerations mirror contractions from head compression.
perOption.r1:c3: Placental insufficiency causes drops that start after the peak.
perOption.r1:c4: This is benign but has a specific cause.
perOption.r2:c2: Abrupt drops come from cord compression.
perOption.r2:c3: Placental insufficiency causes gradual, delayed drops.
perOption.r2:c4: This is not a sign of well-being.
perOption.r3:c3: Delayed drops come from reduced blood flow to the placenta.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match fetal heart rate patterns to their causes.

questions.stem: A client at 40 weeks is placed on the fetal monitor at admission. Over 10 minutes, the fetal heart rate stays between 135 and 150 beats/min. The client asks if this is normal. What is the normal baseline fetal heart rate range?

options.text: 110 to 160 beats/min
100 to 140 beats/min
120 to 180 beats/min
90 to 150 beats/min

rationale.correct: FHR baseline: 110 to 160 beats/min with moderate variability (6 to 25 beats/min).

perOption.a: This is the normal baseline range.
perOption.b: A baseline under 110 is fetal bradycardia.
perOption.c: A baseline over 160 is fetal tachycardia.
perOption.d: A baseline under 110 is fetal bradycardia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the normal fetal heart rate.

questions.stem: A client at 4 cm with the fetus at −2 station has spontaneous rupture of membranes. The fetal heart rate drops to 70/min, and on sterile exam the nurse feels a pulsating cord in the vagina. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand; call for help
Gently push the cord back into the vagina above the presenting part
Wrap the cord in a warm, dry towel
Leave the room to call the provider and the operating room

rationale.correct: Cord prolapse: relieve pressure, knee-chest or Trendelenburg position, oxygen and prepare for urgent cesarean birth.

perOption.a: Relieving pressure on the cord restores blood flow to the fetus; the hand stays in place until birth.
perOption.b: Handling the cord causes vasospasm and reduces blood flow.
perOption.c: Saline-moist gauze is used for an exposed cord, and pressure relief comes first.
perOption.d: The nurse stays and relieves the compression.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 5 cm says, "I think my water just broke," and the nurse sees a large amount of clear fluid on the pad. The fetal head was at −3 station on the last exam. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: The fetal heart rate on the monitor
The color, odor and amount of the fluid
The client's temperature and pulse
The client's pain and need for an epidural

rationale.correct: After rupture of membranes: check the FHR first, then the color, amount and odor of the fluid and the time.

perOption.a: A high presenting part raises the risk of cord prolapse when the membranes rupture.
perOption.b: This is documented, but after the fetal heart rate.
perOption.c: These are checked for infection, but later.
perOption.d: This is not the priority.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 41 weeks has artificial rupture of membranes, and the fluid is thick and dark green. The fetal heart rate is 150/min with moderate variability. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider and have the newborn resuscitation team at the birth
Document the finding as expected, since meconium is common after 40 weeks
Ask the client to push with contractions to shorten the labor
Prepare to suction the newborn's mouth as soon as the head is born

rationale.correct: Meconium-stained fluid: monitor the FHR closely and have a team skilled in newborn resuscitation at the birth.

perOption.a: Meconium-stained fluid means a risk of aspiration and possible fetal stress.
perOption.b: Meconium is more common after 40 weeks, but it still needs reporting and preparation.
perOption.c: The client is not fully dilated.
perOption.d: Routine suctioning on the perineum is no longer recommended.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 6 cm receiving oxytocin has had 7 contractions in the past 10 minutes, each lasting 90 seconds, with the uterus palpating firm between them. The fetal heart rate baseline is 145/min with moderate variability and no decelerations. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the oxytocin infusion
Lower the oxytocin rate by half and recheck in 30 minutes
Continue the infusion, since the fetal heart rate is reassuring
Give terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously

rationale.correct: Tachysystole: more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes; stop or reduce oxytocin, reposition, give fluids and notify the provider.

perOption.a: This is tachysystole; even with a normal tracing, it reduces placental blood flow.
perOption.b: With a firm uterus between contractions, the infusion is stopped first per most protocols.
perOption.c: Tachysystole needs action before fetal distress develops.
perOption.d: This may be ordered if tachysystole persists after stopping the oxytocin.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after an epidural is placed, a laboring client's blood pressure falls from 124/78 to 88/50 mm Hg. The client feels nauseated, and the fetal heart rate baseline is 130/min. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Turn the client to the side and increase the IV fluids
Lay the client flat and raise the legs on pillows
Turn off the epidural infusion and remove the catheter
Give an antiemetic for the nausea and reassess

rationale.correct: Epidural hypotension: side-lying position, IV bolus, notify the provider (ephedrine or phenylephrine) and monitor the FHR.

perOption.a: Epidural blockade causes vasodilation; positioning and fluid restore blood pressure.
perOption.b: The supine position adds vena cava compression.
perOption.c: This is not the nurse's first action.
perOption.d: The nausea is a sign of hypotension.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to hypotension after an epidural.

questions.stem: A client at 8 cm with an epidural for 5 hours has not voided and has had no urinary catheter. The nurse sees a rounded bulge above the pubic bone, and the fetal head has stayed at 0 station for 2 hours. What should the nurse check?

options.text: Whether the bladder is distended and full
The fetal position with Leopold maneuvers
The client's lower extremity reflexes
Whether the epidural catheter has moved

rationale.correct: Check the bladder every 2 hours during labor, especially with an epidural.

perOption.a: An epidural reduces the urge to void; a full bladder can block fetal descent.
perOption.b: The bulge and lack of voiding point to the bladder.
perOption.c: This does not explain the bulge.
perOption.d: This affects pain relief, not descent.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 9 cm who has been calm with breathing techniques is now irritable, nauseated and shaking, and says, "Don't touch me. I can't do this anymore." Contractions are every 2 minutes and last 80 seconds. Which phase of labor does this describe?

options.text: Transition phase of the first stage
Active phase of the first stage
Second stage of labor
Latent phase of the first stage

rationale.correct: Transition: intense contractions, irritability, nausea, shaking and an urge to push.

perOption.a: Transition (8 to 10 cm) is the most intense phase.
perOption.b: The active phase (about 6 to 8 cm) is usually less intense.
perOption.c: This begins at 10 cm.
perOption.d: The latent phase is calmer and the cervix is less dilated.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the transition phase of labor.

questions.stem: A client with gestational diabetes is giving birth to an estimated 4.5 kg baby. The fetal head delivers and then pulls back against the perineum, and the shoulders do not deliver with the next push. The provider calls for help. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Flex the thighs to the abdomen and give suprapubic pressure as directed
Apply firm fundal pressure with the next contraction to push the shoulders out
Apply steady downward traction on the baby's head
Ask the client to stop pushing until the provider is ready

rationale.correct: Shoulder dystocia: call for help, McRoberts (thighs flexed toward the abdomen), suprapubic pressure, no fundal pressure.

perOption.a: McRoberts and suprapubic pressure free the anterior shoulder in shoulder dystocia.
perOption.b: Fundal pressure pushes the shoulder harder against the pubic bone.
perOption.c: This risks brachial plexus injury.
perOption.d: Delay causes fetal hypoxia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client having a trial of labor after a previous cesarean birth is at 7 cm with oxytocin running. The client suddenly reports a tearing pain, contractions stop on the monitor, the fetal head is no longer felt at 0 station and the fetal heart rate drops to 80/min. What does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Uterine rupture
Placental abruption
Rapid progress into transition
Prolapse of the umbilical cord

rationale.correct: Uterine rupture: sudden pain, loss of station, stopped contractions and FHR changes; prepare for emergency cesarean birth.

perOption.a: A prior uterine scar raises the risk; loss of station, stopped contractions and bradycardia are classic.
perOption.b: Abruption causes pain and a rigid uterus, but contractions continue and station is not lost.
perOption.c: Contractions do not stop in transition.
perOption.d: This causes bradycardia, but not tearing pain or loss of station.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Minutes after artificial rupture of membranes, a laboring client says, "Something is wrong," and becomes short of breath and cyanotic. The blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg, the SpO2 is 78% and blood is oozing from the IV site. What does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Amniotic fluid embolism
Supine hypotensive syndrome
Anaphylaxis to the latex in the gloves used for the procedure
Pulmonary embolism from a deep vein clot

rationale.correct: Amniotic fluid embolism: call a rapid response, support airway and circulation, start CPR if needed and prepare for DIC.

perOption.a: Sudden respiratory distress, shock and coagulopathy around membrane rupture are classic.
perOption.b: This does not cause cyanosis, low SpO2 or oozing blood.
perOption.c: This does not explain the coagulopathy.
perOption.d: This does not explain the sudden bleeding.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 6 cm has intense, constant lower back pain between contractions, and the vaginal exam shows an occiput posterior position. The client does not want an epidural yet. Which comfort measure is most helpful?

options.text: Firm counterpressure on the lower back
Lying flat on the back with a pillow under the knees
Staying in one position to save energy
An ice pack placed on the abdomen

rationale.correct: Back labor: counterpressure, hands-and-knees or side-lying positions and a birthing ball.

perOption.a: Counterpressure eases back labor.
perOption.b: This keeps the fetal head against the sacrum and increases pain.
perOption.c: Hands-and-knees or side-lying positions help the fetus rotate.
perOption.d: This does not target back pain.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The baby was born 10 minutes ago and is skin to skin with the parent. The nurse is watching for the third stage of labor. Which group of findings shows that the placenta is separating?

options.text: A gush of blood, the cord lengthening and a firm, rounded uterus
No bleeding, a shortening cord and a soft uterus
A boggy uterus that rises above the umbilicus with heavy bleeding
A sudden rise in blood pressure with severe pain

rationale.correct: Placental separation usually occurs within 30 minutes of birth.

perOption.a: These are the signs of placental separation.
perOption.b: The cord lengthens and a gush of blood is typical.
perOption.c: This suggests uterine atony, not separation.
perOption.d: This is not part of normal separation.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A multiparous client progresses rapidly, and the nurse is alone in the room when the baby's head begins to crown. The provider is 5 minutes away. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Support the perineum, ease the head out slowly and check for a nuchal cord
Apply gentle traction on the head to speed delivery of the shoulders
Ask the client to keep the legs together and pant until the provider arrives
Leave the room to find another nurse or the provider

rationale.correct: Precipitous birth: stay, call for help, support the head, check for a nuchal cord, keep the baby warm and dry.

perOption.a: Controlled delivery prevents tearing, and a cord around the neck must be found.
perOption.b: Traction risks injury to the baby.
perOption.c: Holding back the birth can injure the baby and the client.
perOption.d: The nurse stays with the client.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 31 weeks in preterm labor is receiving terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously. Before the next dose, the nurse reviews the assessment. Which finding requires the nurse to hold the dose and notify the provider?

options.text: Maternal heart rate of 132/min
Blood glucose of 128 mg/dL
Contractions slowing to every 15 minutes
A fine tremor of the hands

rationale.correct: Terbutaline: hold for maternal HR above 120/min, chest pain or dyspnea; watch for hyperglycemia, hypokalemia and pulmonary edema.

perOption.a: Beta-agonists cause tachycardia; most protocols hold the dose for a rate above 120/min.
perOption.b: Mild hyperglycemia is expected with terbutaline.
perOption.c: This is the intended effect.
perOption.d: Mild tremor is a common, expected effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 39 weeks who screened positive for group B streptococcus at 36 weeks is admitted in active labor at 5 cm. The client reports a rash with amoxicillin as a child but no breathing problems. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: IV cefazolin now, ideally at least 4 hours before birth
Oral amoxicillin for the newborn after birth
A scheduled cesarean birth to avoid exposing the baby
No antibiotics, because of the client's penicillin allergy

rationale.correct: GBS-positive: intrapartum IV penicillin; cefazolin for a low-risk allergy; clindamycin or vancomycin for a high-risk allergy.

perOption.a: For a low-risk penicillin allergy, cefazolin protects the newborn from GBS.
perOption.b: Treatment during labor is what protects the newborn.
perOption.c: GBS is not a reason for cesarean birth.
perOption.d: An alternative antibiotic is given.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 39 weeks with ruptured membranes for 20 hours has a temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F). The nurse reviews the fetal monitoring summary for the past hour. Highlight the findings that require intervention.

cells: Two accelerations of 15 beats/min for 15 seconds
Late decelerations with three straight contractions

rationale.correct: Concerning patterns: tachycardia, minimal or absent variability and recurrent late decelerations.

perOption.r4: Fetal tachycardia here may signal maternal infection or hypoxia.
perOption.r5: Minimal variability may signal fetal hypoxia or acidosis.
perOption.r6: Recurrent late decelerations indicate uteroplacental insufficiency.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
